newsitem.title: UK: CWS pretador group calls for end to legal action.
newsitem.headline: CWS pretador group calls for end to legal action.

text.p: Galileo, the group stalking Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS), on Wednesday made a plea to end the legal actions which have thwarted its takeover plans.

The company, set up to bid for the 153-year-old mutually-owned supermarkets to funeral parlour group by entrepreneur Andrew Regan, also said it had complied with a court order issued last Friday to return confidential CWS documents.

"That information had been made available voluntarily to Galileo by an employee of CWS," Galileo said, adding it was not seeking court permission to publish its bid proposal. The court is expected to rule on what it can use on Friday.

Galileo had been preparing a 1.2 billion pound ($2 billion) bid for CWS but was temporarily stopped in its tracks by the group's unexpected legal move. This resulted from information uncovered by the CWS through a firm of private investigators.
Last Thursday CWS suspended two of its senior managers for alleged serious breach of trust after its video surveillance revealed that one of the men had met Regan and an associate.
Galileo, an offshoot of 31-year-old Regan's Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica, said it was making a direct plea to each CWS director to explain its position.

It said it was inviting the CWS board "to consider whether, in preference to continued legal proceedings, it would be in the best interests of members to receive details of the proposal and allow them to reach a decision".

Galileo has not revealed any details of its ambitious plan to break open the labyrinthine structure of the Co-op but has said it would propose a special meeting to convert the group into a limited company which it would then buy.
On Tuesday it emerged that Galileo had arranged a 1.2 billion pound debt facility with Japanese securities giant Nomura. Galileo is known to be backed by a number of City institutions.
Nomura declined to detail this arrangement, but banking sources said the plans had been put together by the firm's innovative principal finance group.
This has been behind a number of high-profile but controversial deals, including a rail rolling stock privatisation and the sale of British Ministry of Defence housing.

Manchester-based CWS owns the profitable Co-operative Bank as well as large British insurer Co-operative Insurance Society (CIS). It is also one of the country's largest undertakers and has other interests ranging from farms to opticians.

The Co-op Bank is seen as the jewel in the CWS crown, with pre-tax profits of 45.5 million pounds, but on Wednesday its chairman Alan Prescott told a meeting of the bank's managers that it was not for sale, repeating a now familiar message.
CWS had a turnover of more than three billion pounds last year but reported a 10 million pound fall in pre-tax profits to 54.1 million pounds.
Its structure encompasses hundreds of thousands of individual members as well as corporate members and a large board of directors. This has been seen as a major obstacle to any take-over attempt.

Regan has been portrayed as an asset-stripper by the Co-op and it is widely accepted that if the Galileo bid were to succeed, parts of the CWS would be sold off, with potential buyers such as Allied Irish Banks already in the frame to buy the Co-op Bank. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
